raw_evidence.label: Why this is interesting now: the Oscars vs. blockbusters gap
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's claim landed at a moment when commentators across film media were arguing that the Academy's choices were drifting away from the films audiences actually watched. By the late 2010s, Oscar telecast ratings had fallen below 30 million viewers (down from a 1998 peak of 57.2 million for Titanic's year). Of the thirteen Best Picture winners between 2011 and 2024, only one — Oppenheimer — crossed $100 million domestic. Best Picture winners increasingly resemble small-to-mid-budget specialty releases, while the films that everyone references (Star Wars, Marvel, Pixar) are mostly absent from the nomination slate. The dataset gives a quantitative angle on this drift: are Best Picture winners still picking up the cultural slipstream that Casablanca, The Godfather and Annie Hall did?

raw_evidence.label: 2015: Spotlight (rank 25) vs The Force Awakens (rank 1) — the steepest mismatch of the 2010s
raw_evidence.content: In 2015, Best Picture went to Spotlight, which sits at rank 25 of its year with 31 references and 0.78% annual_share — the worst rank held by any 21st-century winner. The same year's most-referenced film, Star Wars: The Force Awakens, has 358 references (11.5x more) and 9.0% annual_share. This single year captures the entire thesis: an Academy-celebrated film that the broader culture barely cites, paired with a non-nominated blockbuster that the culture cannot stop referencing.
raw_evidence.code:
# For each oscars_year, get top 3 most-referenced films (the 'people's picks'), and the BP winner
# Show the recent decade (2007-2016) most clearly
def cohort(year):
    sub = df[df['oscars_year'] == year].sort_values('count', ascending=False)
    top3 = sub.head(3)
    winner = sub[sub['result'] == 'W']
    return year, top3[['movie_name','count','result']].values.tolist(), winner[['movie_name','count']].values.tolist() if not winner.empty else []

recent_years = list(range(2007, 2017))
for y in recent_years:
    yr, top3, w = cohort(y)
    print(f"\n{yr}: BP winner = {w}")
    for name, cnt, res in top3:
        flag = '*' if res == 'W' else ('n' if res == 'N' else ' ')
raw_evidence.output: 2015: BP winner = Spotlight 31 refs\n   Star Wars: Episode VII - The Force Awakens (358 refs)

raw_evidence.label: Why this is interesting now: the Oscars vs. blockbusters gap
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's claim landed at a moment when commentators across film media were arguing that the Academy's choices were drifting away from the films audiences actually watched. By the late 2010s, Oscar telecast ratings had fallen below 30 million viewers (down from a 1998 peak of 57.2 million for Titanic's year). Of the thirteen Best Picture winners between 2011 and 2024, only one — Oppenheimer — crossed $100 million domestic. Best Picture winners increasingly resemble small-to-mid-budget specialty releases, while the films that everyone references (Star Wars, Marvel, Pixar) are mostly absent from the nomination slate. The dataset gives a quantitative angle on this drift: are Best Picture winners still picking up the cultural slipstream that Casablanca, The Godfather and Annie Hall did?

# For each oscars_year, get top 3 most-referenced films (the 'people's picks'), and the BP winner
# Show the recent decade (2007-2016) most clearly
def cohort(year):
    sub = df[df['oscars_year'] == year].sort_values('count', ascending=False)
    top3 = sub.head(3)
    winner = sub[sub['result'] == 'W']
    return year, top3[['movie_name','count','result']].values.tolist(), winner[['movie_name','count']].values.tolist() if not winner.empty else []

recent_years = list(range(2007, 2017))
for y in recent_years:
    yr, top3, w = cohort(y)
    print(f"\n{yr}: BP winner = {w}")
    for name, cnt, res in top3:
        flag = '*' if res == 'W' else ('n' if res == 'N' else ' ')

raw_evidence.label: Why this is interesting now: the Oscars vs. blockbusters gap
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's claim landed at a moment when commentators across film media were arguing that the Academy's choices were drifting away from the films audiences actually watched. By the late 2010s, Oscar telecast ratings had fallen below 30 million viewers (down from a 1998 peak of 57.2 million for Titanic's year). Of the thirteen Best Picture winners between 2011 and 2024, only one — Oppenheimer — crossed $100 million domestic. Best Picture winners increasingly resemble small-to-mid-budget specialty releases, while the films that everyone references (Star Wars, Marvel, Pixar) are mostly absent from the nomination slate. The dataset gives a quantitative angle on this drift: are Best Picture winners still picking up the cultural slipstream that Casablanca, The Godfather and Annie Hall did?

raw_evidence.label: What an IMDb 'movie connection' actually counts
raw_evidence.content: Each row's `count` field aggregates IMDb 'movie connections' — crowdsourced records of one title referencing another. IMDb requires that a connection be a deliberate authorial gesture: a quoted line, a visual nod (a poster, T-shirt, on-screen still), a musical parody (the Psycho strings), a reused camera technique, a homage, an actual clip, or a spoof. Generic mentions ('this is like a Bond movie') do not qualify; a 'Casino Royale' poster on a character's wall does. This means each `count` is closer to a curated cultural-footprint score than to raw mentions, but it inherits crowdsourcing biases — popular fan favourites accrue references faster than esoteric titles, and any film a contributor never noticed simply does not exist in the network.

raw_evidence.label: Caveat: the recency problem
raw_evidence.content: Older films have had more decades to accumulate references, so a raw cross-year comparison is not fair. The Economist's chart sidesteps this by ranking *within* each year — annual_share normalises a film's references against the total references to all films released that same year, showing how dominant a single title was in its own cohort. Bioglio & Pensa explicitly chose not to correct for recency, and their results still surface 1939 and 1977 at the top, suggesting the dominance of certain films is not purely an artefact of age.

raw_evidence.label: Bioglio & Pensa 2018: the network-science precedent
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's chart was inspired by a 2018 paper by Livio Bioglio and Ruggero G. Pensa at the University of Turin: 'Identification of key films and personalities in the history of cinema from a Western perspective' (Applied Network Science). They built a directed citation network from the same IMDb connection dataset (after stripping non-film references), covering ~47,000 international films, and computed influence scores by combining four centrality measures (in-degree, closeness, harmonic, PageRank). Their top influential film is The Wizard of Oz (1939), followed by Star Wars (1977) and Psycho (1960) — the same three titles that anchor the top of the Economist's per-year chart. The authors flagged the same caveats: the dataset is heavily Western-biased, and they made no attempt to correct for the 'recency problem' (older films have had more time to be referenced).

raw_evidence.label: Decade-by-decade collapse of the average winner's annual share
raw_evidence.content: Mean annual_share of Best Picture winners peaked in the 1970s at 9.4% — that decade saw The Godfather, Rocky, and Patton each reach #1 in their year, with The Godfather alone capturing 33.7% of all 1972 references. By the 2010s, mean annual_share has collapsed to 1.5% — a 6.4x drop. Median year-rank has roughly tripled, from 3.5 in the 1970s to 8.0 in the 2010s. The percentage of decade winners that hit #1 in their own year falls from 30% (1960s, 1970s) to zero in the 2010s.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_05 ===")
decade_stats = winners.groupby('decade').agg(
    n=('movie_name', 'count'),
    mean_share=('annual_share', 'mean'),
    median_share=('annual_share', 'median'),
    mean_rank=('year_rank', 'mean'),
    median_rank=('year_rank', 'median'),
    pct_top1=('year_rank', lambda s: (s == 1).mean() * 100),
raw_evidence.output: 1970: mean_share=9.44%, median_rank=3.5, pct_top1=30%\n2010: mean_share=1.48%, median_rank=8.0, pct_top1=0%

sentences.context: § The parallel canon
sentences.summary: det_05: Why this is interesting now: the Oscars vs. blockbusters gap. Source: How the Oscars Lost Cultural Relevance — MovieWeb (https://movieweb.com/the-oscars-changed-lost-viewership/) Facts: Oscar viewership fell below 30M by the mid-2010s; 1998 ceremony peaked at 57.2M viewers (Titanic year) Source: Oscar Ratings Sink 9% to 17.8M Viewers — World of Reel (https://www.worldofreel.com/blog/2026/3/17/oscar-ratings-fall-9-to-last-year-wit) Facts: Of the last thirteen Best Picture winners, only Oppenheimer crossed $100M domestic

raw_evidence.label: Why this is interesting now: the Oscars vs. blockbusters gap
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's claim landed at a moment when commentators across film media were arguing that the Academy's choices were drifting away from the films audiences actually watched. By the late 2010s, Oscar telecast ratings had fallen below 30 million viewers (down from a 1998 peak of 57.2 million for Titanic's year). Of the thirteen Best Picture winners between 2011 and 2024, only one — Oppenheimer — crossed $100 million domestic. Best Picture winners increasingly resemble small-to-mid-budget specialty releases, while the films that everyone references (Star Wars, Marvel, Pixar) are mostly absent from the nomination slate. The dataset gives a quantitative angle on this drift: are Best Picture winners still picking up the cultural slipstream that Casablanca, The Godfather and Annie Hall did?

raw_evidence.label: Why this is interesting now: the Oscars vs. blockbusters gap
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's claim landed at a moment when commentators across film media were arguing that the Academy's choices were drifting away from the films audiences actually watched. By the late 2010s, Oscar telecast ratings had fallen below 30 million viewers (down from a 1998 peak of 57.2 million for Titanic's year). Of the thirteen Best Picture winners between 2011 and 2024, only one — Oppenheimer — crossed $100 million domestic. Best Picture winners increasingly resemble small-to-mid-budget specialty releases, while the films that everyone references (Star Wars, Marvel, Pixar) are mostly absent from the nomination slate. The dataset gives a quantitative angle on this drift: are Best Picture winners still picking up the cultural slipstream that Casablanca, The Godfather and Annie Hall did?

raw_evidence.label: Anchor case: Casablanca, the lingua franca of references
raw_evidence.content: Casablanca (1942) is the canonical example of how a Best Picture winner becomes a reference engine. Its IMDb connections page is one of the longest on the site (cited at ~887 entries). Its quoted lines ('Here's looking at you, kid', 'Of all the gin joints…') were officially added to the Oxford Dictionary of 20th Century Quotations in 1999. Direct descendents include The Cheap Detective (1978), Play It Again Sam (1972), and the title of The Usual Suspects (1995). The Economist's column-opening anecdote — Niles in Frasier paraphrasing Rick Blaine — is exactly the type of micro-quote that IMDb crowdsourcers register as a single +1 to Casablanca's count.

raw_evidence.label: Bioglio & Pensa 2018: the network-science precedent
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's chart was inspired by a 2018 paper by Livio Bioglio and Ruggero G. Pensa at the University of Turin: 'Identification of key films and personalities in the history of cinema from a Western perspective' (Applied Network Science). They built a directed citation network from the same IMDb connection dataset (after stripping non-film references), covering ~47,000 international films, and computed influence scores by combining four centrality measures (in-degree, closeness, harmonic, PageRank). Their top influential film is The Wizard of Oz (1939), followed by Star Wars (1977) and Psycho (1960) — the same three titles that anchor the top of the Economist's per-year chart. The authors flagged the same caveats: the dataset is heavily Western-biased, and they made no attempt to correct for the 'recency problem' (older films have had more time to be referenced).

raw_evidence.content: Of the 89 Best Picture winners in the dataset, only 14 (15.7%) were also the most-referenced film of their oscars_year. That set: All Quiet on the Western Front (1930), It Happened One Night (1934), Casablanca (1943), The Lost Weekend (1945), The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957), West Side Story (1961), Lawrence of Arabia (1962), The Sound of Music (1965), Patton (1970), The Godfather (1972), Rocky (1976), The Silence of the Lambs (1991), Titanic (1997), and Gladiator (2000). The post-1990 hit rate is 3 in 27 (Silence of the Lambs, Titanic, Gladiator).
raw_evidence.code:
# also have other films in those years. Find the #1 film per oscars_year and the BP winner.
print("=== ana_09 ===")
top1_by_year = df.loc[df['year_rank'] == 1, ['movie_name','oscars_year','count','annual_share','result']].copy()
winners = df[df['result'] == 'W'][['movie_name','oscars_year','count','annual_share','year_rank']].rename(
    columns={'movie_name':'winner_name','count':'winner_count','annual_share':'winner_share','year_rank':'winner_rank'}
)
merged = winners.merge(top1_by_year, on='oscars_year', how='left', suffixes=('_w','_t'))
merged = merged.rename(columns={'movie_name':'top1_name','count':'top1_count','annual_share':'top1_share','result':'top1_result'})
merged = merged[['oscars_year','winner_name','winner_count','winner_share','winner_rank','top1_name','top1_count','top1_share','top1_result']]
merged['winner_was_top1'] = merged['winner_name'] == merged['top1_name']
print(f"Years where winner was the #1 film: {merged['winner_was_top1'].sum()}/{len(merged)}")
print("\nAll BP winners with their year's #1 film (most recent first):")
print(merged.sort_values('oscars_year', ascending=False).head(25).to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: The 16-year drought: no Best Picture winner has been the most-referenced film of its year since 2000
raw_evidence.content: From oscars_year 2001 through 2016 — 16 consecutive years — no Best Picture winner was the single most-referenced film of its year. The most recent winner to top its own year was Gladiator (2000, 304 references, 6.4% annual share). The longest drought before that was the early-1980s slump (Ordinary People, Chariots of Fire, Gandhi, Terms of Endearment, Amadeus, Out of Africa, Platoon, The Last Emperor, Rain Man — eight winners between 1980 and 1988 with no #1).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_14: The 16-year drought (2001-2016) ---
print("=== ana_14 ===")
recent = winners[winners['oscars_year'] >= 2001]
print(f"From 2001-2016, {len(recent)} BP winners. None were #1 in their year.")
print(f"Mean year_rank: {recent['year_rank'].mean():.1f}")
print(f"Median year_rank: {recent['year_rank'].median():.1f}")
print(f"Worst rank: {recent['year_rank'].max()} ({recent.loc[recent['year_rank'].idxmax(),'movie_name']})")
print(f"Best rank: {recent['year_rank'].min()} ({recent.loc[recent['year_rank'].idxmin(),'movie_name']})")

The most recent winner to top its own year was Gladiator (2000, 304 references, 6.4% annual share). The longest drought before that was the early-1980s slump (Ordinary People, Chariots of Fire, Gandhi, Terms of Endearment, Amadeus, Out of Africa, Platoon, The Last Emperor, Rain Man — eight winners between 1980 and 1988 with no #1).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_14: The 16-year drought (2001-2016) ---
print("=== ana_14 ===")
recent = winners[winners['oscars_year'] >= 2001]
print(f"From 2001-2016, {len(recent)} BP winners. None were #1 in their year.")
print(f"Mean year_rank: {recent['year_rank'].mean():.1f}")
print(f"Median year_rank: {recent['year_rank'].median():.1f}")
print(f"Worst rank: {recent['year_rank'].max()} ({recent.loc[recent['year_rank'].idxmax(),'movie_name']})")
print(f"Best rank: {recent['year_rank'].min()} ({recent.loc[recent['year_rank'].idxmin(),'movie_name']})")
